title: HHS / ONC HTI-1 Final Rule: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability — Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing (89 FR 1192)

policy_extraction.issuing_body: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS / ONC)
covered_actors: Health IT developers participating in the ONC Health IT Certification Program (especially developers of Health IT Modules certified to 45 CFR § 170.315(b)(11) Decision Support Interventions, the Base EHR definition, § 170.315(g)(10) FHIR APIs, and developers meeting Insights Condition thresholds of at least 50 hospital sites or 500 individual clinician users)

ONC-Authorized Certification Bodies (ONC-ACBs) and ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratories (ONC-ATLs) certifying, testing, and conducting surveillance over certified Health IT Modules under 45 CFR Part 170

Actors subject to 45 CFR Part 171 Information Blocking regulations (health IT developers of certified health IT, health information networks/exchanges, and health care providers) and healthcare organizations adopting CEHRT for CMS Medicare Promoting Interoperability and MIPS programs
prohibited_practices: Information blocking: practices by a health IT developer of certified health IT, health information network/exchange, or health care provider that are likely to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), unless required by law or covered by an exception in 45 CFR Part 171 (§ 171.103)

Inhibiting a customer's timely access to interoperable health IT certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program, including failing to update and provide Health IT Modules certified to revised certification criteria within regulatory timeframes (§ 170.402(a)(5) and (b)(3))

Discriminating when determining whether requestors are similarly situated under the Manner Exception Exhausted condition based on whether the requestor is an individual, health care provider type/size, or a competitor (§ 171.204(a)(4)(iv))

evidence.quote: For evidence-based decision support interventions and Predictive Decision Support Interventions supplied by the health IT developer as part of its Health IT Module, the Health IT Module must enable a limited set of identified users to access complete and up-to-date plain language descriptions of source attribute information specified in paragraphs (b)(11)(iv)(A) and (B) of this section.

For developers of Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(b)(11), starting January 1, 2025, and on an ongoing basis thereafter, review and update as necessary source attribute information in § 170.315(b)(11)(iv)(A) and (B), intervention risk management practices described in § 170.315(b)(11)(vi), and summary information provided through § 170.523(f)(1)(xxi).

Where applicable, summary information of the intervention risk management practices listed in § 170.315(b)(11)(vi) is submitted by the health IT developer via publicly accessible hyperlink that allows any person to access the summary information directly without any preconditions or additional steps.
Source attributes listed in paragraphs (b)(11)(iv)(A) and (B) of this section must be supported.
Intervention risk management practices must be applied for each Predictive Decision Support Intervention supplied by the health IT developer as part of its Health IT Module.

We have also finalized in § 170.315(b)(11)(vi) that intervention risk management (IRM) practices must be applied for each Predictive DSI supplied by the health IT developer as part of its Health IT Module, including requirements to subject Predictive DSIs to risk analysis and risk mitigation related to validity, reliability, robustness, fairness, intelligibility, safety, security, and privacy.

compliance_deadlines: 2024-02-08: Final rule effective date and Incorporation by Reference (IBR) approval date (89 FR 1192)

2024-12-31: Deadline for health IT developers certified to § 170.315(a)(9) to certify to § 170.315(b)(11) DSI criterion, apply IRM practices, submit public IRM summary hyperlinks to ONC-ACBs (§ 170.523(f)(1)(xxi)), and publish FHIR service base URLs (§ 170.404(b)(2))

2025-01-01: Expiration of legacy CDS criterion § 170.315(a)(9); § 170.315(b)(11) becomes mandatory in Base EHR definition (§ 170.102); Assurances Maintenance of Certification ongoing review/update duty (§ 170.402(b)(4)) takes effect

policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Under the ONC Health IT Certification Program (45 CFR Part 170), non-compliance with § 170.315(b)(11) DSI transparency, IRM, Assurances Maintenance of Certification (§ 170.402), Real World Testing (§ 170.405), or Insights Condition (§ 170.407) subjects developers to ONC-ACB surveillance, ONC Direct Review (§ 170.580), mandatory corrective action plans (potentially including notification to all customers), and suspension or termination of Health IT Module certification—jeopardizing Base EHR / CEHRT status required for customer participation in CMS Medicare Promoting Interoperability and MIPS payment programs. Separate violations of 45 CFR Part 171 Information Blocking rules are subject to HHS OIG enforcement, statutory civil monetary penalties for developers/HINs/HIEs, and appropriate disincentives for health care providers under PHSA § 3022(b)(2).
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Published January 9, 2024 (89 FR 1192) and effective February 8, 2024 under the HITECH Act and 21st Century Cures Act. Establishes the first binding U.S. federal regulation setting algorithm transparency and AI risk management obligations for clinical and operational healthcare AI/ML ('Predictive Decision Support Interventions' in 45 CFR § 170.102, explicitly encompassing supervised, semi-supervised, and self-supervised models including LLMs and generative AI, while excluding purely unsupervised similarity models). Replaces legacy CDS (§ 170.315(a)(9)) with DSI (§ 170.315(b)(11)) in the Base EHR definition starting January 1, 2025, requiring: (1) structured 'source attributes' (31+ metadata fields functioning as clinical model nutrition labels covering intended use, out-of-scope cautions, training data criteria and demographic/SDOH/health-status representativeness, fairness approaches, external/local validation, quantitative performance, and update schedules); (2) Intervention Risk Management (IRM) practices covering NIST AI RMF-aligned risk analysis across eight characteristics (validity, reliability, robustness, fairness, intelligibility, safety, security, privacy), risk mitigation, and data governance for all developer-supplied Predictive DSIs; (3) public hyperlink disclosure of IRM summary practices via ONC-ACBs on CHPL (§ 170.523(f)(1)(xxi)); (4) ongoing Assurances Maintenance of Certification review/updates (§ 170.402(b)(4)) and annual Real World Testing (§ 170.405); and (5) complementary interoperability, USCDI v3, SMART App Launch 2.0 / 1-hour API revocation, Insights Condition reporting (§ 170.407), and Part 171 Information Blocking / TEFCA Manner Exception rules.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The HHS/ONC HTI-1 Final Rule is dominantly framed around consumer and public safety, grounding its Predictive Decision Support Intervention transparency, risk-management, and interoperability mandates in protecting patients from clinical harm, reducing medical errors, improving sepsis and care outcomes, and ensuring healthcare AI tools are fair, appropriate, valid, effective, and safe. Fundamental rights forms a deeply intertwined secondary frame anchored in advancing 'health equity by design,' rooting out algorithmic bias and discrimination against historically underserved and marginalized communities (implementing Executive Orders 13985 and 14091), and strengthening patient data privacy, access, and authorization-revocation rights. Innovation enablement plays a major supporting role: ONC calibrates transparency guardrails without rigid performance thresholds to build public trust, unlock wider adoption of promising clinical AI tools, and foster a vibrant standards-based FHIR application ecosystem. Economic competitiveness serves as a distinct supporting frame tied to Executive Order 14036, curbing information blocking and market consolidation while correcting information asymmetry so healthcare markets reward higher-quality predictive models.

evidence_spans.quote: It also promotes the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence through transparency and improves patient care through policies that advance standards-based interoperability and EHI exchange, which are central to the Department of Health and Human Services' efforts to enhance and protect the health and well-being of all Americans.

The finalized DSI requirements will improve transparency, promote trustworthiness, and incentivize the development and wider use of fair, appropriate, valid, effective, and safe Predictive DSIs to aid decision-making in healthcare.

In this final rule we apply the concept of health equity by design to bring transparency to the quality and performance of intelligence and machine learning-based decision support tools in healthcare.

Section 8 of
E.O. 14091
requires agencies to “prevent and address discrimination and advance equity for all” and to “consider opportunities to prevent and remedy discrimination, including by protecting the public from algorithmic discrimination.”

Thus, we sought to establish appropriate guardrails for information transparency about Predictive DSIs that do not undercut the value that could be offered to patients and clinicians from such promising technologies.
evidence_spans.source_section: III.C.5 Objectives of the Policies To Address Predictive Modeling in DSI

evidence_spans.quote: We believe that increased transparency into the performance of models and risk management practices related to their development will result in (1) wider uptake of Predictive DSIs overall due to greater certainty about the intervention's performance, and (2) selection of fairer, more appropriate, more accurate, more effective and safer models through greater information on the available choices.
evidence_spans.source_section: VII.C.1.a Regulatory Impact Analysis — DSI Benefits

evidence_spans.quote: The implementation of the new information blocking provisions detailed in section IV of this final rule promote innovation, encourage market competition, and address consolidation in the interest of the patient to advance interoperability, improve transparency, and support the access, exchange, and use of EHI.
We believe that increased transparency will lead to an effective market for predictive models that adequately incentivizes and rewards high-quality models.
